TV and Media

Scott Pelley told the New York Times that CBS News leadership instructed him to “inject falsehoods” that aligned with the Trump administration into a piece on immigration enforcement in Minnesota.

By Greta Kaul

Fired “60 Minutes” correspondent Scott Pelley accused new CBS editor-in-chief Bari Weiss of trying to insert “falsehoods and bias” into a report about the Renee Good and Alex Pretti killings in Minneapolis, he said in an interview with the New York Times published Sunday.

Last week, CBS fired Pelley, who worked at the network for nearly 40 years, after he clashed with managers over the direction of the network and the show. Pelley’s firing comes as other former “60 Minutes” journalists have accused managers of seeking to insert political bias into coverage.

Pelley’s firing followed a staff meeting in which he questioned the qualifications of new “60 Minutes” executive producer Nick Bilton and accused Weiss of “murdering” the show, the New York Times reported.

Weiss said Pelley was fired because trust had been broken after his comments at the staff meeting.

In a statement, Pelley accused managers of telling him to “inject falsehoods and bias into a politically sensitive story.”

In the interview Sunday, Pelley specified he was referring to a February piece about protests against Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota.

In Pelley’s telling, he and his team had interviewed Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), who was holding hearings on Metro Surge tactics, and built a story around the killings of Good and Pretti and the protests in Minnesota.

“We culled together a lot of video of protesters screaming in the faces of officers because we were going to talk about the killing of Pretti and the killing of Good, and it seemed to me important to tell the audience about the entire context‚" Pelley told the New York Times’ Lulu Garcia-Navarro.

Pelley said the piece went through screenings and rewrites and was approved to run. Four hours after a noon EST deadline — “60 Minutes” airs at 7 p.m. EST — Pelley said his team got a note from Weiss.

“Two of the things in the email include, can we make the protesters look more violent?” he said. “Now, I’m paraphrasing. I don’t have the quote, but that’s what was communicated to me. And the other thing, Renee Good’s car. You need to describe her as driving toward the officer."

Pelley said he felt the team had gone out of its way to show the context of the protests, and they had gone over video of Good’s killing repeatedly to make sure their reporting was accurate.

He said he felt Weiss was asking for revisions to fit the narrative of President Donald Trump and his administration.

“The event was not as the president said and not the way Bari Weiss remembered it,” he said.

Ultimately, Pelley aired the story without those changes. In a statement in response to Pelley’s account, a CBS News spokesperson told the New York Times, “In an email, Bari made four points in the course of editorial back-and-forth. They had no political motivation and were proposed solely to make the piece as strong, fair, and accurate as possible. As is frequently the case in any newsroom that operates with collaboration, not everything she raised made it into the final piece.”

Pelley said the interference remained an issue, as did the chaos he said Weiss caused with the after-deadline email.

Jane Kirtley, professor emerita at the University of Minnesota who was the longtime director of the Silha Center for the Study of Media Ethics and Law, emphasized that Pelley’s account is one side of the story, supplemented by brief statements from CBS, but she said the incident raises questions about CBS’ independence.

“There can be good faith disagreement about what happened during Operation Metro Surge, but as the old saying goes, ‘You’re entitled to your own opinion, but not your own facts,’ " Kirtley said.

Weiss, the founder of the Free Press media company and a New York Times Opinion writer before becoming editor-in-chief at CBS News, was hired to change the prism through which the news organization operates, Kirtley said.

But Pelley’s interview and accounts from other “60 Minutes” journalists who have raised bias concerns and been fired or not had contracts renewed raise questions about the journalistic credibility of the show and the network under Weiss, Kirtley said.

“It’s about truth and accuracy,” she said. Editorial staff exists to keep reporters honest, pushing them to ensure their own accuracy, Kirtley said, but several accounts now raise concerns that Weiss has gone beyond that, asking for stories to be approached from an angle pushed by the Trump administration.

If that’s the case, that’s a problem — regardless of what administration is in power, Kirtley said.

"The whole purpose of the First Amendment, I think most people would say, would be to hold government to account," Kirtley said.
